extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (epistemology, aesthetics, theory of humor)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of distinctions between abstract (rational) knowledge and feeling, the limits and uses of reason in practice and art, a theory of the ludicrous (laughter, wit, folly, pun), and an account of science and the faculty of judgment. Intended as philosophical analysis rather than empirical rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational knowledge ("wissen")
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract cognition is 'rational knowledge' (wissen): the result of reason, the permanent possession in concepts of what has been previously known in perception; abstract knowledge reproduces for thought what was received in another way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rational/abstract knowledge does not extend knowledge but gives it form that is preservable, communicable, and applicable in practice. Examples: translating perceptive knowledge of levers, pulleys, arches, curves into abstract concepts enables construction and cooperative activity; differential calculus changes intuitive knowledge of curves into abstract form useful for application. Notes on limits: abstract concepts approximate perception (mosaic vs painting) and may fail to capture fine perceptual distinctions; arithmetic (numbers/time) is needed to render space-relations into communicable abstract knowledge (see further guidance on numbers vs space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling (negative definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept 'feeling' denotes a merely negative content: whatever is present in consciousness 'is not a concept' and therefore falls under feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sphere of 'feeling' is extremely wide and heterogeneous — religious feeling, sensual pleasure, moral feeling, bodily sensation (touch, pain, colour, sound), hate, pride, æsthetic feeling, love, etc. — united only by being non-conceptual. The author suggests using the German 'empfindung' (sensation) for bodily feeling as a sub-species. This negative definition explains frequent misunderstandings about 'feeling'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason's one-sidedness in classifying non-conceptual states as 'feeling'
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason, because it deals in concepts and names, tends to class under the single concept 'feeling' every modification of consciousness that is not an abstract concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classificatory one-sidedness of reason has produced confusion and led to the postulation of a special faculty of feeling and speculative theories of it. The passage warns that conceptual vantage points make what is near appear positive and what is farther off appear negative, producing broad grouping errors (analogy with national/sectarian naming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses and limits of abstract knowledge in practice and art
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract knowledge is crucial for planning, communication, cooperative work, and long-term application, but it never exactly corresponds to perceptive knowledge; in some activities reflection can hinder performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: preservability, communicability, reliable application across times and agents, indispensible for coordinating multiple agents (e.g., constructing machines or buildings). Disadvantages/anti-patterns: for immediate perceptual skills (billiard-playing, fighting, tuning, singing, virtuoso performance, physiognomy, pathognomy), reflective abstraction can divide attention and spoil intuitive execution. In art, concepts are 'unfruitful' for the essential creative matter; they can only direct the technical part. Moral action and genuine virtue proceed from will/feeling rather than from abstract reflection; reason plays a subordinate role in preserving resolutions and providing maxims for consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of laughter (the ludicrous) — core principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of laughter in every case is the sudden perception of the incongruity between a concept and the real objects which have been thought through it in some relation; laughter is the expression of this incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter results from a paradox/unexpected subsumption: either two or more disparate real objects are thought through one concept, or a concept is applied to an object whose other properties show the concept to be inadequate. The greater the correctness of the subsumption from one point of view and the more glaring the incongruity from another, the stronger the ludicrous effect. The account covers both verbal and action-based forms and connects ludicrousness to surprise and contradiction of expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between wit and folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit and folly are two species of the ludicrous. Wit: two or more very different real objects are known and are intentionally identified through one concept (intentional subsumption). Folly: the concept is present first, and action applies it to reality, revealing the object's divergence (unintentional subsumption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit is typically expressed in words and is intentional; folly is typically shown in actions and is unintentional (though folly can appear in words when merely expressing intended but unexecuted actions or mistaken judgments). The jester/clown artfully combines awareness of diversity with the appearance of folly (intentionally disguising wit as folly). This provides a practical distinction for analyzing humorous instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedantry as a form of folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedantry arises when a person lacks confidence in his own understanding and insists on guiding everything strictly by general concepts, rules, and maxims — 'clinging to form' replaces apprehension of the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: pedantry produces awkwardness and failure in life, lifeless mannerism in art, and leads to false or inapplicable outcomes in ethical action because abstract maxims may only half apply or conflict with individual character. The author criticises moral systems (e.g., Kantian moral formalism) for encouraging a kind of moral pedantry. Anti-pattern: overreliance on abstract maxims in contexts requiring fine particular judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pun (calembourg) and equivocation as spurious wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The pun brings two different concepts, by accident of language, under one word; it is a spurious, more superficial kind of wit compared with true witticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison: in witticism identity is in the concept and difference in reality; in pun difference is in the concepts and identity in the (accidental) terminology. Unintentional misunderstandings (quid pro quo) are related to pun as folly is to wit. Uses: puns often serve to express obscenity (double entendre). Example pattern: deafness-based misunderstandings may produce laughter like folly does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science defined by systematic form (from general to particular)
rubrics_metrics.description: A science begins with a concept that marks off the class of objects and strives for complete abstract knowledge of that class by systematic descent from the general to the particular; systematic form and subordination of principles characterize science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features: sciences use nested concept-spheres and determine relations among them so that the members are determined by deduction; completeness of a science consists in maximum subordination and minimal coordination of first principles. Examples: mathematics (axioms and deduced propositions), classificatory sciences (zoology, botany, physics, chemistry) have more subordination; history has little subordination and is therefore rational knowledge but not science in the strict sense. Methodological note: science's aim is form and completeness, not necessarily greater certainty; primary judgments from perception are central to building science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the faculty of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty of judgment is the power of rightly and accurately carrying into abstract consciousness what is known in perception; it mediates between understanding and reason and establishes primary judgments that are the basis of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgment creates primary truths directly from perception, which serve as the strongholds of science; deficiency in judgment is 'silliness' — failure to grasp partial identity or difference among concepts. Kant's distinction of reflecting vs subsuming judgment applies (from perceived objects to concepts, or vice versa). Exceptional strength of judgment advances science, though ordinary reasoning suffices for deduction and demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers (time) as medium for abstracting space-relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations of space cannot be directly translated into abstract concepts except through temporal quantities (numbers); numbers alone can be expressed in abstract concepts that accurately correspond to quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: arithmetic (number/time) is the universal science of quantity; geometry must be translated into arithmetic to be communicable, precise, and applicable in practice. This explains the difficulty of mathematics when rendering three-dimensional spatial relations into one-dimensional temporal conceptual terms and motivates analytic methods (calculus, logarithmic tables) for abstract expression of spatial relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary judgments versus demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all truth requires demonstration; every demonstration rests on an undemonstrated truth; directly established truths drawn from perception are as preferable to demonstrated truths as water from a spring to water from an aqueduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological consequence: science depends on primary judgments founded in perception (or pure a priori perception in mathematics) rather than on an infinite regress of demonstrations. The insistence that only demonstrated judgments are true is a perverted opinion; demonstrations cannot replace the primary perceptual judgments that illuminate and ground science.
